question: The arrest in April 2024 of two people suspected of spying for China in Germany comes in the wake of other examples, involving Russia in particular, and highlights the threats from foreign intelligence services to our democracies, our economic interests and even the freedom of those who live in the European Union.

Collaboration among counter-espionage services and intelligence agencies is essential in tackling foreign interference. Within the EU, this collaboration involves the European Union Intelligence and Situation Centre (INTCEN), Europol and even the Intelligence Directorate of the European Military Staff (EUMS-INT).

The way in which their work and competences are shared out is somewhat confusing for the general public Moreover, some argue that this collaboration is at times hampered by a lack of trust between certain national intelligence services and agencies. Does the Commission intend to propose measures to improve this trust and enhance cooperation in the fight against espionage and intelligence? 1.
In particular, will it strengthen Europol’s counter-espionage role?
Will it establish a genuine European intelligence agency to complement a reinforced Europol?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.7.2024) National security remains the sole responsibility of each Member State according to Article 4(2) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). Under its current mandate1 and mission2, the European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) is competent for certain forms of cross-border crime3 including terrorism.

In this context, the European Counter Terrorism Centre (ECTC), located at Europol, represents a cornerstone in EU-level cooperation in national counter terrorism efforts, and is the first centre of its kind created as part of the EU’s counter terrorism security policy.

Moreover, Europol has developed a specific secure communication platform (Secure Information Exchange Network Application or SIENA)4 to allow counter-terrorism authorities handle of restricted content on counter-terrorism. The European Union Intelligence and Situation Centre (INTCEN) has been connected to SIENA since September 2022.

Concerning cooperation between Europol and Member States’ domestic intelligence services, Europol has established contacts at strategic level with the Counter-Terrorism Group (CTG) which is part of the ‘Club de Berne’, a forum of European intelligence services. The Commission does not plan to strengthen Europol’s counter-espionage role or to establish a European intelligence agency.

The Commission will continue to increase its awareness of hostile foreign actors’ attempts to undermine EU democracy and values5 and work with Member States and other relevant EU institutions, bodies and agencies to ensure appropriate response.
1 Regulation (EU) 2016/794 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 May 2016 on the European
Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol).) (Europol Regulation).

2 Article 88 TFUE: ‘‘Europol’s mission shall be to support and strengthen action by the Member States’ police authorities and other law enforcement services and their mutual cooperation in preventing and combating serious crime affecting two or more Member States, terrorism and forms of crime which affect a common interest covered by a Union policy’. 3 Annex I of Europol .Regulation.

4 The Secure Information Exchange Network Application (SIENA) is a platform that enables the swift, secure and user-friendly exchange of operational and strategic crime-related information among law enforcement authorities.

5 For example, following the activation of the integrated political crisis response (IPCR) on foreign interference in European elections, the Commission prepares Integrated Situational Awareness and Analysis (ISAA) reports, contributing to increased preparedness and a fast, coordinated response at EU level.
